## Today

**Today's view: a role-play. We are the trial statistician of one randomized
trial with a survival endpoint, from protocol to submission.**

* Plan the trial: protocol, estimand, SAP, sample size, group sequential design
* Collect the data: CRF, raw data, SDTM, ADaM
* Report the results: TFL shells, tables and figures, the R packages behind them
* Monitor the trial: interim analyses, p-values, conditional power
* Submit the package: datasets, metadata, reviewer's guides

Every number on these slides comes from the code in `r gh("lab/")`. You can run
the code on Posit Cloud, on your own computer, or with Claude.

::: notes
This lecture is a role-play, not a methods lecture. We act as the trial
statistician and use the survival methods from this course on one trial. Ask
students to open the repository now so they can follow along.
:::

## Glossary

Clinical trials use many acronyms. The slides spell out each acronym at first
use. Full list: `r gh("lab/docs/00_glossary.md")`.

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
* **SAP**: Statistical Analysis Plan
* **CRF**: Case Report Form; **EDC**: Electronic Data Capture
* **CDISC**: Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium
* **SDTM**: Study Data Tabulation Model (collected data)
* **ADaM**: Analysis Data Model (analysis-ready data)
* **TFL**: Tables, Figures and Listings
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
* **PFS**: Progression-Free Survival; **OS**: Overall Survival
* **ORR**: Objective Response Rate
* **TEAE**: Treatment-Emergent Adverse Event
* **DMC**: Data Monitoring Committee
* **IA**: Interim Analysis
* **CP**: Conditional Power
:::
::::

# Part 1 · The map of a trial {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Who does what, and our example trial

## The statistician's role in a trial

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box lead"><b>Protocol</b>objectives, endpoints, sample size</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>SAP + shells</b>all analyses planned in advance</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>CRF / EDC</b>collect what the SAP needs</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Raw data</b>EDC export + vendor files</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>SDTM</b>standard format for collected data</div>
</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box review"><b>ADaM</b>datasets ready for analysis (the statistician writes the specifications)</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>TFLs</b>tables, figures, listings</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>Clinical study report</b>results and interpretation</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Submission</b>datasets and reports for the regulator</div>
</div>
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box dashed"><b>Interim analysis</b>same ADaM + TFL programs on a data cut &rarr; Data Monitoring Committee &rarr; continue / stop</div>
</div>
```

[<span class="legend-lead"></span> statistician leads &nbsp;&nbsp; <span class="legend-review"></span> statistician specifies and reviews]{.small}

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The statistician is responsible for**: design, sample size, SAP, shells,
ADaM specifications, interim plan, interpretation.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The statistician works with**: clinicians (endpoints), data managers (CRF,
data cleaning), statistical programmers (SDTM, ADaM and TFL code), regulatory
affairs (submission).
:::
::::

::: notes
The interim analysis can change the course of the trial; this possibility is
the reason for group sequential designs. Programmers write most of the code,
but the statistician decides what the code must do and approves the results.
:::

## Our example trial: CDISCPILOT01

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
* Data from **pharmaverse**: the CDISC SDTM/ADaM pilot study (xanomeline patch
  vs placebo), plus **synthetic RECIST 1.1 tumour assessments**
* In this lecture, the study is a **two-arm oncology trial**:
  High Dose vs Placebo, randomized 1:1
* Our **source data** (`r gh("lab/data/source/")`): the pilot cut to our two
  arms and exported as CSV (comma-separated values) files. Every lab program starts there.
* `r nrow(adsl)` patients screened, `r sum(adsl$ITTFL == "Y")` randomized
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
adsl |>
  dplyr::mutate(Arm = factor(TRT01P, levels = c(ARM_LEVELS, "Screen Failure"))) |>
  dplyr::count(Arm, name = "Patients") |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
All data are synthetic test data from pharmaverse. We use no real patient data.
:::

# Part 2 · Planning {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Protocol, estimand, SAP, sample size, group sequential design

::: notes
Every later step carries out a decision made here.
:::

## Protocol: the parts the statistician writes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
| | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| Primary | **PFS**: randomization to first progression (RECIST 1.1, investigator) or death |
| Key secondary | **OS**: randomization to death from any cause |
| Secondary | **ORR**: best overall response CR or PR |
| Secondary | **DCR**: best overall response CR, PR or SD |
| Safety | TEAEs (MedDRA), labs (CTCAE grades) |

[RECIST: Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; CR / PR: complete / partial response; SD: stable disease; DCR: disease control rate; MedDRA: Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities; CTCAE: Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events]{.tiny .muted}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Also written by the statistician**

* Hypotheses and alpha (next slide)
* Design: 1:1, event-driven, two interim analyses
* Sample size and assumptions
* Analysis populations and methods (summary)
* Multiplicity strategy for the secondary endpoints
* Interim analyses and DMC charter

Full text: `r gh("lab/docs/01_protocol_synopsis.md")`
:::
::::

## The hypothesis: what does HR 0.6 mean?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
$$
H_0: \mathrm{HR} = 1 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1: \mathrm{HR} < 1
$$

* One-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%
* Design HR `r DESIGN$hr`: the drug lowers the hazard of progression or death by 40%
* Exponential survival: median = log(2) / hazard, so HR = median (Placebo) / median (High Dose)
* Placebo median `r DESIGN$median_control` months → High Dose median **`r sprintf("%.1f", median_exp)` months**
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.4
p_hypothesis
```
:::
::::

## The estimand (ICH E9(R1))

An estimand defines **what** we estimate, before we decide **how** to estimate. ICH: International Council for Harmonisation.

| Attribute | PFS, High Dose vs Placebo |
|---|---|
| Population | All randomized patients (intention-to-treat, ITT) |
| Treatment | High Dose vs placebo, added to best supportive care |
| Variable | Time to progression (RECIST 1.1) or death |
| Intercurrent events | Stops treatment early: *treatment policy* (keep scanning) · Death: part of the endpoint (*composite*) · New anticancer therapy: *hypothetical* (censor before the new therapy) |
| Summary measure | Hazard ratio (Cox model), tested by log-rank |

::: {.takeaway}
Censoring rules are not programming details: the rules define how the estimand
handles intercurrent events. Write the rules in the SAP, then program the rules
exactly as written.
:::

## SAP: decide everything before unblinding

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. **Analysis populations**: ITT set (all randomized, as randomized); safety set (all who received study drug, as treated)
2. **Analysis visit windows**: study day; a window around each scheduled visit; which record counts when two fall in one window
3. **Baseline characteristics**: baseline = last value before the first dose; how each variable is collected and summarized; partial dates imputed in ADaM only, never in SDTM
4. **Efficacy**: endpoint derivations and **censoring rules**; test and model; multiplicity; interim analyses (timing, boundaries, futility)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
5. **Sensitivity analyses**: for example PFS by independent central review
6. **Safety**: treatment-emergent window, MedDRA coding, CTCAE grades, exposure
7. **Computation conventions**: confidence interval (CI) methods (log-log for the median, Clopper-Pearson for rates), ties (Efron), rounding, software versions. R and SAS defaults differ, so the SAP names each method.

TFL shells come with the SAP. Final version before database lock (DBL) and before anyone sees unblinded data. Excerpt: `r gh("lab/docs/02_sap.md")`
:::
::::

## Analysis sets become ADSL flags

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Set | Definition | Flag |
|---|---|---|
| ITT | All randomized, **as randomized** | `ITTFL`, `TRT01P` |
| Safety | All who received study drug, **as treated** | `SAFFL`, `TRT01A` |

[ADSL: subject-level analysis dataset, one row per patient]{.small .muted}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
adsl |>
  dplyr::filter(ITTFL == "Y") |>
  dplyr::count(`Randomized (TRT01P)` = TRT01P, `Received (TRT01A)` = TRT01A, name = "Patients") |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Every patient received the randomized treatment, so both sets have the same arms.
`r n_never_81`
High Dose patients stopped during the 54 mg start and never reached 81 mg. These
patients started the High Dose regimen, so they stay High Dose for safety.
:::

## PFS censoring rules (SAP section 6.1)

| Situation | Date | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Progression documented (RECIST 1.1) | Date of the first scan showing progression | **Event** |
| Death before progression | Date of death | **Event** |
| No progression, no death | Last adequate tumour assessment | Censored |
| No post-baseline assessment, no death | Randomization | Censored |
| New anticancer therapy before progression | Last adequate assessment before the new therapy | Censored |
| Event after two or more missed scans | Last adequate assessment before the gap | Censored (sensitivity) |

[Adapted from US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance *Clinical Trial Endpoints for the Approval of Cancer Drugs and Biologics* (2018). Part 3 turns this table into code.]{.small .muted}

## Step 1. How many events? (fixed design)

Schoenfeld's formula (1:1 randomization, log-rank test):

$$
d = \frac{4\,(z_{1-\alpha} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{(\log \mathrm{HR})^2}
= \frac{4\,(1.960 + 0.842)^2}{(\log 0.6)^2} \approx `r round(events_fixed, 1)`
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r design-schoenfeld, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
* A fixed design (no interim analysis) needs **`r ceiling(events_fixed)` events**
* Power comes from the number of **events**, not from the number of patients
* Information for the log-rank test ≈ events / 4
:::
::::

## Step 2. From events to patients

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r design-fixed-n, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Patients = events / P(a patient has an event)**

* Assumptions: placebo median PFS `r DESIGN$median_control` months (placebo arms of refractory colorectal cancer trials such as CORRECT and RECOURSE), HR `r DESIGN$hr`, 24-month enrollment, 3-month minimum follow-up, 25% dropout by month 3
* P(event by month `r DESIGN$accrual_months + DESIGN$followup_months`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", p_event)`
* `r round(fixed$d, 1)` / `r sprintf("%.2f", p_event)` = `r round(fixed$n, 1)` → **`r n_fixed` patients**
* More patients or longer follow-up: the same events come sooner
:::
::::

## Why a group sequential design?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
* Look at the data **before** the planned end: stop early for efficacy, or for futility
* Each look adds a chance of a false positive result: split the one-sided 2.5% alpha across the looks
* **Alpha spending function** (Lan-DeMets, O'Brien-Fleming type); $t$ = events observed / events planned:

$$
\alpha(t) = 2\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\right]
$$

* Very little alpha is spent early, so the final boundary stays close to 1.96
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_boundary
```
:::
::::

## Step 3. Group sequential design in {gsDesign} {.code-small}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r design-gsd, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
boundary_tbl |>
  dplyr::select(Analysis, `Events (planned)`, `Expected month`, `Efficacy boundary (Z)`,
                `Nominal one-sided p`, `HR at boundary`) |>
  tab(16)
```

* `r round(events_fixed, 1)` events × inflation factor `r sprintf("%.3f", inflation)` = `r round(max(gs$n.I), 1)` → **`r target_events` events**; **`r 2 * n_per_arm` patients** (`r n_per_arm` per arm)
* Interim analyses at **`r ia_events[1]`** and **`r ia_events[2]`** events
* Futility is **non-binding** and based on conditional power (Part 5), so the design has efficacy boundaries only
:::
::::

## The analyses are triggered by events, not dates

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
p_events
```
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
* Count the **total** PFS events: both arms pooled, **blinded**
* Interim 1 at `r ia_events[1]` events, interim 2 at `r ia_events[2]`, final at `r target_events`
* The calendar month is only a forecast; update the forecast as events come in
* Data cut-off date = date of the event that reaches the target
:::
::::

## Power analysis

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.6
p_power
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
power_tbl |>
  tab(16)
```

* With `r target_events` events, power falls fast if the true HR is larger than `r DESIGN$hr`
* The HR is the most important and least certain assumption: justify the HR with data from earlier trials
* Proportional hazards is also an assumption; a delayed treatment effect (common with immunotherapy) reduces power
:::
::::

# Part 3 · Data standards {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

CRF → raw data → SDTM → ADaM

::: notes
Students rarely see raw data; show the formats and the QC story.
:::

## Collect only what the SAP needs

| SAP needs | Source | Raw file in `lab/data/raw/` | SDTM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized arm and date | IRT vendor transfer | `irt.csv` | DM.ARM, DS |
| Age, sex, race | Demographics CRF | `dm.csv` | DM |
| First / last dose, dose received | Exposure CRF | `ex.csv` | EX, DM |
| Progression | Tumour response CRF | `rs.csv` | RS |
| Death, end of study | End of Study CRF | `ds.csv` | DS |
| Adverse events | Adverse event CRF + MedDRA coding | `ae.csv` | AE |
| Concomitant medications | Concomitant medication CRF + WHODrug coding | `cm.csv` | CM |
| Laboratory values | Central lab transfer | `lb.csv.gz` | LB |

[IRT: Interactive Response Technology (randomization system); CM: concomitant medications; WHODrug: World Health Organization Drug Dictionary]{.small .muted}

## The annotated CRF: Adverse Event page

| CRF question | CRF field (CDASH) | Raw value | SDTM variable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adverse event term | `AETERM` | APPLICATION SITE ERYTHEMA | `AETERM` |
| Start date | `AESTDAT` | 03 JAN 2014 · UN JAN 2014 | `AESTDTC` = "2014-01-03" · "2014-01" |
| Severity | `AESEV` | Mild / Moderate / Severe | `AESEV` = MILD / MODERATE / SEVERE |
| Serious? | `AESER` | Yes / No | `AESER` = Y / N |
| Relationship to study drug | `AEREL` | None / Remote / Possible / Probable | `AEREL` |
| (coding team) | `AETERM_PT`, `AETERM_SOC` | APPLICATION SITE ERYTHEMA | `AEDECOD`, `AEBODSYS` |
| (derived) | | | `AESEQ`, `AESTDY` |

[CDASH: Clinical Data Acquisition Standards Harmonization, a standard for CRF field names that map to SDTM. PT: preferred term; SOC: system organ class.]{.small .muted}

## How we made the raw data

Our source data contain SDTM only. The lab rebuilds raw data from SDTM
(**reverse engineering**): the code undoes the derivations that the SDTMIG
(SDTM Implementation Guide) asks a sponsor to do.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
1. Remove derived variables: `--SEQ`, `--DY`, `USUBJID`, `AGE`, reference dates
2. ISO 8601 dates → CRF text
3. Controlled terminology → CRF display text
4. Keep dictionary codes as "coding" columns
5. Reshape findings data into the layout of CRF and vendor files
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r raw-date-helpers, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::::

## SDTM: a short overview

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**One dataset per domain**, grouped in classes

* Special purpose: **DM** (demographics)
* Interventions: **EX** (exposure), **CM** (medications)
* Events: **AE** (adverse events), **DS** (disposition)
* Findings: **LB** (labs), **VS** (vitals), **RS** / **TU** / **TR** (tumour response, identification, results)
* Trial design: TA, TV, TS ...
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Common conventions**

* `USUBJID`: unique across all studies of the sponsor
* Dates in ISO 8601 (`--DTC`), partial dates stay partial
* Study day `--DY`: **no day 0**
* `--SEQ`: unique record number within patient
* Controlled terminology (CT): `SEX` is `"F"` or `"M"`
* Non-standard variables go to SUPPQUAL (supplemental qualifiers), e.g. `SUPPDM`
:::
::::

## Quality control (QC): compare with an independent version

```{r}
qc_summary |>
  tab(22)
```

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**DM `RFENDTC`, patient 01-710-1083.** The reference data use the date of the
end-of-study page. Our rule uses the date of the event (death). This difference
is a **specification ambiguity**: fix the specification, not only the code.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**AE and CM: no differences.** All `r nrow(ae_sdtm)` AE records and
`r nrow(cm_sdtm)` CM records match the reference in every variable. Each
difference that does appear needs a root cause before the data are used.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Regulated outputs are checked by independent double programming: two
programmers, one specification, then a comparison with {diffdf} or SAS PROC COMPARE.
:::

## QC in industry practice

* **Clean logs**: the production and the QC programs run with no errors and no warnings
* **Dataset QC compares everything**, not only the values: variables, types,
  lengths, labels, formats and every value ({diffdf}, SAS PROC COMPARE)
* **Output QC**: every number in every TFL is compared with the QC version
* **Batch run**: one script reruns all production and QC programs and collects
  the logs and the compare results (here: `r gh("lab/run_all.R")`)
* **Compliance**: CDISC conformance checks (for example Pinnacle 21) on SDTM and ADaM

::: {.takeaway}
QC is planned work with its own programs and records, not a last look before delivery.
:::

## ADaM: ready for analysis and traceable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Principles (ADaM Implementation Guide, ADaMIG)**

* Ready for analysis: one procedure call gives the result
* Traceable: every value can be traced back to SDTM
* Documented by metadata (define.xml)

**Structures**

* **ADSL**: one row per patient
* **BDS** (Basic Data Structure): one row per patient × parameter × time point. ADLB, ADRS, **ADTTE**
* **OCCDS** (Occurrence Data Structure): ADAE, ADCM
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
| SDTM sources | ADaM dataset | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| DM, DS, VS, SUPPDM | **ADSL** | one row per patient |
| RS + ADSL | **ADRS** | BDS (response by visit, best overall response, progression) |
| ADSL + ADRS | **ADTTE** | BDS (PFS, OS) |
| AE + ADSL | **ADAE** | OCCDS |
| CM + ADSL | **ADCM** | OCCDS |
| LB + ADSL | **ADLB** | BDS (with CTCAE grades) |

[Built with {admiral} (pharmaverse): one function per derivation rule.]{.small .muted}
:::
::::

## Why {admiral}?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
* Built **across the industry**: many pharmaceutical companies develop and use {admiral} together (pharmaverse)
* Built like engineering software: unit tests, code review, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), regular releases
* Used for several years in many companies, including in submissions
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**More mature than the SDTM tools. Why?**

* ADaM input is **always SDTM**: one standard
* SDTM input varies: EDC exports, CDISC ODM (Operational Data Model), CDASH forms, many vendor formats
* So raw → SDTM tools (for example {sdtm.oak}) are younger and more study-specific
:::
::::

## ADSL: add the variables our SAP needs {.code-small}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r adsl-derive, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

## TFL shells are part of the SAP

:::: {.columns}

**Table 14.2.1** Progression-free survival (ITT set)

| | Placebo (N=xx) | High Dose (N=xx) | Total (N=xx) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Events, n (%) | xx (xx.x%) | xx (xx.x%) | xx (xx.x%) |
| Censored, n (%) | xx (xx.x%) | xx (xx.x%) | xx (xx.x%) |
| Median, months (95% CI) [a] | x.x (x.x - x.x) | x.x (x.x - x.x) | x.x (x.x - x.x) |
| HR vs Placebo (95% CI) [b] | | x.xx (x.xx - x.xx) | |
| One-sided p (log-rank) | | x.xxxx | |

[[a] Kaplan-Meier, Brookmeyer-Crowley CI (log-log). [b] Cox model.]{.tiny}
:::

* Written **before** any data exist and agreed by the statistician, clinicians and programmers
* Shells fix the numbering (ICH E3: 14.1 baseline, 14.2 efficacy, 14.3 safety), titles, population, rows, columns (with a **Total** column), statistics, decimals and footnotes
* Programmers write code to match the shell; QC compares the output with the shell
* All shells: `r gh("lab/docs/04_tfl_shells.md")`
:::

## The endpoint depends on who reads the scan, and when

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
* Progression is a judgement. Here every scan has three reads: the investigator and two independent radiologists
* The two radiologists disagree on `r reader_disagree$differ` of `r reader_disagree$visits` visits (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reader_disagree$differ / reader_disagree$visits)`); an **adjudicator** accepts one read: the blinded independent central review (BICR) result
* Reads, queries and data cleaning take time, so a patient's PFS status at a given calendar date can still change
* So the event count at a data cut-off, and even the cut-off date, can move
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
review_tbl |>
  tab(18)
```
[First progression per patient: investigator vs BICR (`r sum(review_tbl$Patients)` patients with tumour assessments).]{.small .muted}
:::
::::

## The log-rank test, step by step

$$
\chi^2 = \frac{\left(\sum_j (O_{1j} - E_{1j})\right)^2}{\sum_j V_{1j}},\qquad
E_{1j} = d_j \frac{n_{1j}}{n_j},\qquad
V_{1j} = d_j \frac{n_{1j}\, n_{0j}\,(n_j - d_j)}{n_j^2\,(n_j - 1)}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
logrank_parts |>
  tab(20)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
* $V$ = `r round(logrank_var, 2)`, so $\chi^2$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", lr$obs[2] - lr$exp[2])`² / `r round(logrank_var, 2)` = **`r sprintf("%.3f", pfs_hi$chisq)`** (1 df), p = `r fmt_p(pfs_hi$p_chisq)` (two-sided)
* For the one-sided test: $Z = (E - O)/\sqrt{V}$ = **`r sprintf("%.3f", pfs_hi$z)`** for High Dose, one-sided p = **`r fmt_p(pfs_hi$p_one_sided)`**
:::
::::

## What can we claim? Multiplicity

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box lead"><b>1. PFS</b>primary: the gatekeeper</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>2. OS</b>key secondary</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>3. ORR</b>secondary</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>4. DCR</b>secondary</div>
</div>
```

* The order is fixed in the SAP before unblinding. Pass a step (reject H0 at one-sided 2.5%) → test the next step; fail a step → **stop**

```{r}
hier_tbl |>
  tab(18)
```

* PFS boundary at the final, from the **actual** information (`r paste(ia_events_obs, collapse = " and ")` events at the interims, `r pfs_hi$events` at the final): Z ≥ `r sprintf("%.3f", z_final)`. PFS is not rejected, so all later results are **descriptive**

## TFL production in practice

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Long before database lock**

* Shells approved together with the SAP; ADaM specifications (one row per variable, with derivation)
* **Dry runs** on blinded or dummy-treatment data
* The trial goes on, so the outputs are **re-run periodically** (DMC, safety reports, ad-hoc requests), not only at the final analysis

**Quality checks**

* Independent double programming; clean logs
* Data compliance checks (Pinnacle 21) for CDISC conformance and data quality
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Reproducibility**

* Version control (for example git): depends on each company's practice
* For R submissions, locked package versions with **renv** are the usual practice (see the R Consortium submissions working group)
* One command reruns everything (`r gh("lab/run_all.R")`)

**Reviews**

* **Statistical review**: consistent with the SAP? Consistent across tables, figures and documents (events in 14.2.1 = ADTTE = DMC report)? Right denominators?
* **Clinical review**: do the results make clinical sense?
* **Cosmetic review**: titles, footnotes, decimals, layout
:::
::::

# Part 5 · Interim analysis {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Boundaries, p-values, conditional power, the DMC report

::: notes
Ask the room for a recommendation before showing the final result.
:::

## Steps of an interim analysis

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box review"><b>Track events</b>total events, both arms, blinded</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Cut-off date</b>date of the event that reaches the target</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Clean data</b>up to the cut-off date</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>Re-run</b>the same ADaM and TFL programs on the cut data</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>Independent statistician</b>unblinded closed report</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box lead"><b>DMC</b>closed session, recommendation</div><div class="arrow">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="box review"><b>Sponsor</b>receives only the recommendation: continue / modify / stop</div>
</div>
```
* The sponsor's study team stays **blinded**: a separate, independent team does the unblinded work
* Open session: pooled data and trial conduct. Closed session: efficacy and safety by arm.

## The data cut in code: one program for every cut

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r adam-datacut, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r adtte-interim, opts.label = "code"}
```

* Interim 1: cut-off **`r format(ia_dco[1])`**, `r looks$events[1]` events
* Interim 2: cut-off **`r format(ia_dco[2])`**, `r looks$events[2]` events
:::
::::

## Interim 1: result and boundary

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
p_ia_boundary
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
* Information fraction `r ia$events` / `r target_events` = `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ia$events / target_events)`: Lan-DeMets spending computes the boundary **at the actual fraction**
* HR `r sprintf("%.2f (95%% CI %.2f, %.2f)", ia$hr, ia$hr_lower, ia$hr_upper)`
* Z = `r sprintf("%.3f", ia$z)`, one-sided p = `r fmt_p(ia$p_one_sided)`
* Efficacy needs Z ≥ `r sprintf("%.3f", z_eff[1])` (p ≤ `r sprintf("%.4f", pnorm(-z_eff[1]))`): **not crossed**
:::
::::

## Conditional power and the futility rule {.code-small}

$$
\mathrm{CP}(\theta) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{c_K \sqrt{I_K} - Z_k \sqrt{I_k} - \theta\,(I_K - I_k)}{\sqrt{I_K - I_k}}\right),
\qquad I \approx \frac{\text{events}}{4},\quad \theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r ia-conditional-power, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
cp_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(theta = round(theta, 3), `Conditional power` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * `Conditional power`)) |>
  tab(20)
```

{gsDesign} `gsCP()` gives `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cp_gs_design)` under the design HR, the same result.

::: {.takeaway}
Futility rule (SAP, non-binding): consider stopping if CP under the current
trend is below 10%. CP under the design HR is the most optimistic number:
always show the current trend too.
:::
:::
::::

## Table IA.1 The DMC closed report (primary endpoint)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
slide_rt(t_ia_1, 15)
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**What would you recommend?**

* Efficacy boundary: not crossed
* CP under the current trend: `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cp_trend)`, below 10%: the **futility rule is met**
* The DMC would recommend stopping for futility. The rule is non-binding: the sponsor makes the final decision
:::
::::

## Every look, the same rules

```{r}
looks_tbl |>
  tab(16)
```

* Futility is non-binding: continuing does not increase alpha. For teaching, we also ran interim 2 and the final analysis on all data: the conclusion does not change
* **Sample size re-estimation (SSR)**: when CP is promising but lower than planned, some designs increase the target events at an interim. SSR must be pre-specified and must protect alpha (for example the Cui-Hung-Wang weighted test)

## Other content of the DMC report

:::: {.columns .small}
::: {.column width="50%"}
* Enrollment, disposition, protocol deviations, by arm
* Exposure and dose modifications
* Adverse events, serious adverse events, deaths, labs
* Efficacy: Table IA.1, Kaplan-Meier by arm (Figure IA.1), conditional power

**The DMC does not meet only at interim analyses.** Between interim
analyses, the DMC holds regular **safety reviews** (for example every 6
months): safety data only, by arm, no efficacy.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
p_km_ia
```
:::
::::

# Part 6 · Deliverables and submission {background-color="#1D4F91" .part-title}

Deliverables during the trial, datasets, metadata, reviewer's guides

## Submission is not the only deliverable

| Deliverable | When | Receiver | The statistician's work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interim analysis | At the planned number of events | DMC | Boundaries, conditional power, closed report (Part 5) |
| Safety reviews | Every few months, at each DMC or SRC meeting | DMC; Safety Review Committee (SRC) | Safety tables by arm, listings of deaths and serious adverse events |
| DSUR | Every year, for each drug in development | Regulators | Exposure and cumulative safety summaries |
| Ad-hoc requests | Any time, often with a short deadline | Regulators, DMC, medical team, publications | New tables, figures or analyses outside the SAP |
| CSR and submission | After database lock | Regulators | Final TFLs, datasets, metadata, reviewer's guides |

[DSUR: Development Safety Update Report (ICH E2F). CSR: Clinical Study Report.]{.small .muted}

::: {.takeaway}
One set of ADaM datasets and TFL programs serves all these deliverables: build
the programs once, then run the programs on each new data cut.
:::

## What the FDA receives

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(ectd_tree)
```

[eCTD: electronic Common Technical Document; module 5 holds clinical study reports and data.]{.small .muted}

[Our lab keeps data as **CSV**: easy to check (any software, git diff), but CSV keeps no types or labels. A submission uses **XPT** files described by define.xml.]{.small}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
* **XPT**: SAS transport files, version 5 (names ≤ 8 characters, labels ≤ 40)
* **define.xml**: metadata for every dataset, variable, code list and derivation
* **aCRF**: annotated CRF
* **cSDRG / ADRG**: Clinical Study Data Reviewer's Guide (SDTM) / Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide (ADaM)
* Programs for the primary and key secondary results
* Conformance checks (Pinnacle 21) with explanations

:::
::::

## Metadata-driven XPT files with {xportr}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r sub-xportr, opts.label = "code"}
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
xpt_check |>
  head(12) |>
  tab(18)
```
:::
::::

## R in regulatory submissions

* The FDA does not require any specific software (Statistical Software Clarifying Statement, 2015). The FDA requires work that is documented and reproducible.
* The R Consortium submission pilots sent the FDA TFLs, a Shiny app and ADaM datasets, all built in R (github.com/RConsortium/submissions-wg)
* What reviewers need from an R submission:
  * package versions (`renv.lock`, `sessionInfo()`) and installation steps
  * programs that run on the submitted datasets and reproduce the numbers in the CSR
  * an ADRG that explains these items
* Many companies now use both R and SAS; double programming in two languages is common

## Five key messages {.larger}

1. **Write the SAP like code.** Every rule must have only one meaning; QC finds the gaps (`RFENDTC`).
2. **Power comes from events.** Design, predict and monitor events, not patients.
3. **Traceability.** CRF field → raw → SDTM → ADaM → the number in the table.
4. **Interim analyses are triggered by events and reuse the final programs on a data cut**; the boundaries use the actual information.
5. **Futility by conditional power.** CP depends on the assumed effect: report CP under the design effect and under the current trend.
